I know so little, and it troubles me—just a little.”

“Tell me what it is.”

“I have a cousin, my only relative, and an orphan like me, whom I love very much. She's five years younger than I am and lives in a farmer's house in the south. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of what has happened to me. I can't write—and even if I could, how could I tell her? It's better this way.”

“Yes, yes. Better this way.”

“This is what I've been thinking as we travelled here, and what I'm still thinking now, looking into your kind, strong face, which gives me such courage: if the Republic really helps the poor, so that they suffer less hunger and less hardship of every kind, she may live for many years. She might even grow old.”

“What then, my gentle sister?”

“Do you think,” she asks, her uncomplaining eyes, so full of endurance, filling with tears, her lips opening a little wider and trembling, “that the wait will seem long to me, until she joins me in that better land where I trust you and I will both find merciful shelter?”

“It cannot, my child. There is no Time there, and no suffering.”

“You give me so much comfort! I know so little. Should I kiss you now? Has the moment come?”

“Yes.”

She kisses his lips; he kisses hers. They solemnly bless each other. Her thin hand is steady as he lets it go, and her patient face shows only a sweet, radiant resolve. She goes just before him—is gone. The knitting women count Twenty-Two.

“‘I am the Resurrection and the Life,’ says the Lord. ‘Whoever believes in me will live, even though he dies; and whoever lives and believes in me will never die.’”

The murmur of countless voices, the countless faces turning upward, the pressure of footsteps at the crowd's edges that sends it surging forward like one great swell of water—all flashes away. Twenty-Three.

That night, people throughout the city said his was the most peaceful face ever seen there. Many added that he had looked sublime and prophetic.

Not long before, one of the most remarkable people to die beneath the same blade—a woman—had asked, at the foot of that scaffold, for permission to write down the thoughts that inspired her. Had he expressed his own thoughts, and had they been prophetic, they would have been these:

“I see Barsad and Cly, Defarge, The Vengeance, the Juryman, the Judge, and long lines of new oppressors who have risen through the destruction of the old, dying beneath this instrument of retribution before its present use comes to an end.

‘Oh, forget my hat! I want Virginia!’ cried the young Duke, laughing, and they galloped on to the railway station. There Mr. Otis asked the stationmaster whether anyone matching Virginia's description had been seen on the platform, but learned nothing. The stationmaster did, however, send telegrams in both directions along the line and promised that everyone would watch closely for her. Mr. Otis bought the young Duke a hat from a cloth merchant who was just closing his shutters. Then he rode off to Bexley, a village about four miles away. He had been told that gypsies often stayed there because of the large common beside it. They woke the village policeman, but he had no information for them. After riding across the whole common, they turned for home. They reached the Chase at about eleven, exhausted and almost heartbroken. Washington and the twins were waiting at the gatehouse with lanterns, since the avenue was very dark. No trace of Virginia had been found. The gypsies had been overtaken on Brockley meadows, but she was not with them. They explained that they had left so suddenly because they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and hurried away for fear of arriving late. In fact, they were deeply upset to hear that Virginia was missing. They felt very grateful to Mr. Otis for letting them camp in his park, and four had stayed to help look for her. The carp pond had been searched with dragging equipment, and every part of the Chase had been carefully examined, without success. It was clear that, for that night at least, they could not find Virginia. Mr. Otis and the boys walked toward the house in utter misery, while the groom followed with the two horses and the pony. In the hall stood a group of frightened servants. Poor Mrs. Otis lay on a sofa in the library, almost frantic with fear and worry, while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with eau-de-cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted that she eat something and ordered supper for everyone. It was a sad meal. Almost nobody spoke, and even the twins were frightened and quiet, for they loved their sister dearly. When they had finished, Mr. Otis sent them all to bed despite the young Duke's pleading. He said there was nothing more they could do that night. In the morning he would telegraph Scotland Yard and ask them to send detectives immediately.

“Oh, your father can certainly spare you if your mother can. Daughters never matter quite so much to a father. And if you stay another full month, I can take one of you as far as London. I'm going there for a week in early June, and since Dawson doesn't mind riding on the carriage's outside seat, there will be ample room for one of you. Indeed, if the weather is cool, I wouldn't object to taking both of you, as neither of you is large.”

“You are very kind, madam, but I believe we must keep to our original plan.”

Lady Catherine seemed to accept this. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak my mind, and I cannot bear the thought of two young women travelling alone in a hired carriage. It is most improper. You must arrange for someone to go. I dislike that sort of thing more than anything. Young women should always have suitable protection and attendants, according to their position in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted that two male servants accompany her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley and Lady Anne, could not properly have appeared otherwise. I pay the closest attention to all such matters. You must send John with these young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I'm glad I thought to mention it, because letting them go alone would reflect very badly on you.”

“My uncle is sending a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle! He employs a male servant, does he? I'm very glad someone in your family thinks about these things. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, naturally. Mention my name at the Bell, and they will look after you.”

Lady Catherine had many more questions about their journey. Since she did not supply all the answers herself, Elizabeth had to pay attention, which she considered fortunate. Her mind was so preoccupied that otherwise she might have forgotten where she was. She had to keep her reflections for the hours she spent alone. Whenever she had that opportunity, she surrendered to them with immense relief. Not a day passed without a solitary walk during which she could indulge in all the pleasure of painful recollections.

She was well on her way to learning Mr. Darcy's letter by heart. She examined every sentence, and her feelings toward its author sometimes changed dramatically. Remembering the manner in which he had addressed her still filled her with indignation. But when she considered how unfairly she had judged and reproached him, her anger turned upon herself, and she felt compassion for his disappointed hopes.
